## Principle

Process control rests on a simple idea: a process can be held at a desired value by feedback. The story begins with the controlled variable — a level, a temperature, a pressure, a flow — which is measured continuously. The measurement is compared with the set point, the value that the variable is required to hold. The difference between the set point and the measurement is known as the error, and it is the error that serves as the input to the controller. Working from the error, the controller computes an output, and the output moves a final element, which changes a manipulated variable — a stream, a duty, or some similar quantity — that acts back on the process itself. The loop is closed: every change in the controlled variable finds its way back, through the measurement, to the controller.

Crucially, the feedback employed in control is negative in sign. When the controlled variable rises, the controller produces an action that opposes the rise, driving the manipulated variable in the direction that brings the controlled variable back towards the set point. The loop therefore corrects disturbances it was never told about. A change in the feed, a change in the ambient conditions, a surface that gradually fouls — any influence that pushes the controlled variable away from its set point generates an error, and the error generates the correction. No model of the disturbance is required; the measurement simply reports its combined effect.

The simplest form of controller action is proportional action, under which the change in the output is proportional to the error, the constant of proportionality being the controller gain. Proportional action on its own, however, leaves an offset once a disturbance has settled, because a changed manipulated variable can only be held by a changed output, and a changed output can only be produced by an error that continues to stand. Integral action addresses this shortcoming by continuing to move the output for as long as any error persists, thereby removing the offset. Derivative action responds to the rate at which the error is changing, and anticipates where the error is heading. Underpinning all of this is a deliberately simple working model: the process is treated as though it responds in proportion to a change in its input, with a lag and a dead time for its dynamics. The sections that follow build the loop up from that model before turning to where the model breaks down.

## Equipment

A control loop is assembled from a measuring element, a transmitter, a controller and a final element, connected in that order around the process. The measuring element senses the controlled variable: a level element is displaced or loaded by the liquid, a resistance thermometer changes resistance with temperature, and a pressure element deforms under the pressure applied to it. The transmitter converts the response of the measuring element into a standard signal that can be carried over a distance, and it is the signal, rather than the variable itself, that the remainder of the loop handles.

The controller receives the signal, forms the error against the set point, and computes the output. In a modern plant, the controller is one function among many in a distributed control system, and its settings — the gain, the integral time and the derivative time — are entered as part of the system's configuration rather than being dialled in on the instrument itself. The set point is supplied by the operator, or from a higher-level calculation supervising the loop.

The final element converts the controller output into the actual change in the manipulated variable. It usually takes the form of a control valve: an actuator moves the valve stem, while a positioner compares the actual stem position with the position demanded by the output and drives the actuator until the two agree, so that the stem follows the output in spite of friction and the forces exerted on the plug by the process. An important design consideration is that the valve is specified to fail in the safe direction should its power supply be lost: a valve that must be shut to protect the process fails closed, whereas a valve that must stand open to protect the process fails open. The choice is made loop by loop, from the consequences of the valve sitting in its failed position while the process is unattended.

## Worked example

Consider a tank fed by a stream whose flow the operator does not control, with liquid drawn off through a control valve in the outlet line. The level in the tank plays the role of the controlled variable, the outflow that of the manipulated variable, and a level controller holds the level at its set point by moving the valve as required. Initially the tank runs steadily: inflow and outflow are equal, the level stands at the set point, the error is zero, and the valve sits part-open at the opening the steady outflow requires.

Now suppose the feed rate rises, and stays higher. Inflow now exceeds outflow, and the level begins to climb. The measurement climbs with the level, the error changes as the measurement moves above the set point, and the controller responds by opening the valve further. As the valve opens, the outflow rises. The level continues to climb while inflow still exceeds outflow, although the climb slows as the outflow approaches the new inflow, until outflow and inflow come back into balance with the valve at a wider opening and the level at a standstill.

The standstill, however, does not occur at the set point. Under proportional action alone, the wider valve opening is held by a larger controller output, and that larger output can only be produced by an error that continues to stand, so the level settles above the set point and remains there: exactly the offset the principle section predicts, in precisely the predicted form. If the same loop is fitted with integral action, the picture changes: the output continues to creep while the offset persists, the valve opens further still, the level is brought back to the set point, and the error is driven to zero, after which the output holds its new value with no error left to sustain it. The example thus bears out the principle in both forms: proportional action holds the new balance at the price of an offset, while integral action removes the offset by removing the error on which it stands.

## Limits

The model underlying the principle section is a simplification, and its shortcomings mark the limits of what a single loop can achieve. The model treats the process as though it responds in proportion to its input. Real processes are under no such obligation: the gain of a heat exchanger changes with throughput, the gain of a tank level changes with the cross-section of the tank wherever the section is not uniform, and a valve passes a flow that depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening. A controller tuned at one operating point has been tuned for one particular gain, and its performance deteriorates as the process moves away from that point — sluggish at one extreme of the range, oscillatory at the other.

The model also allows for dead time, but treats the response as beginning cleanly once the dead time has elapsed. Where dead time makes up a large part of the overall response — a long pipe run between the valve and the measurement, or a composition obtained by an analyser through a sample line — the controller is condemned to act on information that is already old. Corrections arrive late, overshoot, and are corrected late in their turn; the loop oscillates however carefully it has been tuned, and the genuine remedy is to relocate the measurement or accept a slower loop, rather than to raise the gain.

Saturation imposes a harder limit still. A valve fully open can pass no more, and a valve fully shut can pass no less; once the travel of the final element is exhausted, the loop is effectively open and the variable uncontrolled, regardless of what the controller computes. The remaining limit is set by the measurement. Noise on the signal is passed to the controller as though it were genuine movement of the variable, and derivative action is particularly prone to amplifying it, so the quality of the measurement caps the tightness of control the loop can usefully employ.

Finally, loops do not operate in isolation. The level loop of the worked example shares its tank with every other loop that moves the same streams, and each loop's correction becomes the next loop's disturbance. A treatment confined to single loops can state this limit plainly but cannot remove it: interacting loops must be detuned against one another, or the control problem reformulated with the interaction inside it.

Feedback control, as presented in this chapter, is the correction of a measured variable by an error-driven loop built from a measuring element, a controller and a final element. Its great strength is that the disturbance itself never needs to be known. Set against that strength are its limits: the linearity the model assumes, the dead time the loop cannot remove, the travel of its final element, and the quality of its measurement.
